subject: Help with error fitting join model with inlabru (group location and size)

messages.author: 8b77562d54aed3c9
messages.subject: Help with error fitting join model with inlabru (group location and size)
parts:
Hi,

My research question is related to the location and size of schools of fish on a coral reef.
In setting up my analysis I'm trying to initially replicate "10_1d_groups.R" from the inlabru workshop using a subset of my data ("shoal_sizes.GeoJSON") but with two spatial dimensions instead of one used in the example.

Unfortunately, I can't seem to get the joint model of both location and size to fit and get the following error:
"GMRFLib version 3.0-0-snapshot, has recived error no [12]
    Reason    : The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
    Message   : Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
    Function  : GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern
    File      : approx-inference.c
    Line      : 2947
    RCSId     : file: approx-inference.c  hgid: 0bed76828f01  date: Tue Sep 03 11:21:49 2019 +0300"

This error happens on the third iteration of attempting to fit the model (the process takes 4 iterations to fit the model of group size assuming a constant rate). With the first two iterations appearing to work fine.

When I run the model with verbose INLA output the last report before the error is:
"max.logdens= -23816786.5519 fn= 4 theta= 2.3671 0.3698 2.6927 0.5062  range=[-593.04 1.99]". So my guess is the max.logdens is going to -Inf and breaking something? For reference the same type of line from the first iteration is: "max.logdens= -531.3581 fn= 1 theta= 2.5914 -0.7448 2.5994 0.0783  range=[-25.12 1.27]" which is similar for both the first and second iteration. 

Another difference I noticed between the second (works) and third (breaks) iteration is the initial theta values (iteration 2: theta =  2.591 -0.7448 2.589 0.07834; iteration 3: theta =  2.452 0.3332 2.585 0.2928) which I presume is related to the dramatic change in the max.logdens between the two iterations?

Unfortunately I'm not sure if I'm getting this result because I'm making some mistake creating the model and going from 1D to 2D spatial component. Or if there's something I'm doing wrong relating to the mesh or something else (priors, control settings, etc.). I'm new to inlabru and inexperienced with INLA in general so please forgive me if there is some silly mistake.

Any help or advice would be hugely appreciated! Thank you. I've attached the subsetted data, the relevant sampling area data, and R script I'm working with isolated to just the relevant parts.
Jason

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help with error fitting join model with inlabru (group location and size)
parts:
Hi,

there's a potential problem with your mesh, in that it doesn't cover the entire site. This can be fixed with something like this:

boundary.loc <- as(shoals, "SpatialPoints")
boundary.site <- SpatialPoints(INLA::inla.sp2segment(site)$loc,
                               proj4string = CRS(SRS_string = wkt(site)))
boundary <- list(
  inla.nonconvex.hull(coordinates(boundary.loc), 1.46),
  inla.nonconvex.hull(rbind(coordinates(boundary.loc),
                            coordinates(boundary.site)),
                      1.5))

But even with that you'll likely run into the same iteration issue. It looks like another case of where the new robust iteration method for inlabru is needed. It's not yet available in the code, but I'm working on it. Expect a few weeks until it may be available in the devel version. For now, your best bet is to use tighter priors, which sometimes helps (but is not ideal, since it does change the model...).

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help with error fitting join model with inlabru (group location and size)
parts:
Are _all_ the object&data coordinates in the same coordinate system? Then there should essentially only be a factor 10^6 difference in estimated intensity (not sure if your plots show intensity or log-intensity?).  If all the objects are in the same coordinate system as the mesh, then adding the crs should change the intensity by a factor 10^6 to convert between m^2 and km^2.  If one of the objects is in a different coordinate system to the others, then you must have a crs on the mesh to make all the mappings work correctly. 
From what I remember in your code, the objects all do have the same CRS, so it's likely that the result differences are still due to numerical optimisation instability.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Help with error fitting join model with inlabru (group location and size)
parts:
Setting E=1e9 should in theory just change the interpretation of the intercept parameter in the model, which should change by around log(1e9), depending on the prior. If the prior precision for the intercept covariate is unchanged, it won’t be exactly that.
In practice, it may also have an impact on the numerics.
For large domains, I typically recommend converting the whole space to kilometres instead of metres, since this also impacts the numerical accuracy.

Finn

Hi,

there's a potential problem with your mesh, in that it doesn't cover the entire site. This can be fixed with something like this:

boundary.loc <- as(shoals, "SpatialPoints")

Finn

parts: For this smaller problem looking at just one site that I'm using to understand the model and software better the area is ~10m x 20m. The full project has 12 similarly sized sites spread along ~12km slightly curved coastline. Do either of those qualify as a large domain?

On Friday, September 18, 2020 at 1:57:23 PM UTC-5 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
Setting E=1e9 should in theory just change the interpretation of the intercept parameter in the model, which should change by around log(1e9), depending on the prior. If the prior precision for the intercept covariate is unchanged, it won’t be exactly that.
In practice, it may also have an impact on the numerics.
For large domains, I typically recommend converting the whole space to kilometres instead of metres, since this also impacts the numerical accuracy.

Finn

On 18 Sep 2020, at 19:51, jdse...@gmail.com <jdse...@gmail.com> wrote:

﻿
Yes everything is in the same coordinate system and the plots are of intensity not log-intensity.

I set E = 1e9 and that seems to at least visually remove the difference between the mesh with and the one without the CRS. Does that change the model or simply help deal with the numerical instability?

On Friday, September 18, 2020 at 1:27:03 PM UTC-5 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
Are _all_ the object&data coordinates in the same coordinate system? Then there should essentially only be a factor 10^6 difference in estimated intensity (not sure if your plots show intensity or log-intensity?).  If all the objects are in the same coordinate system as the mesh, then adding the crs should change the intensity by a factor 10^6 to convert between m^2 and km^2.  If one of the objects is in a different coordinate system to the others, then you must have a crs on the mesh to make all the mappings work correctly. 
From what I remember in your code, the objects all do have the same CRS, so it's likely that the result differences are still due to numerical optimisation instability.

Finn
